content: Dapsone (topical) is an anti-infective agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of acne vulgaris. It is intended for external topical use only and should not be used orally, ophthalmically, or intravaginally. After gently washing and drying the skin, a pea-sized amount of Dapsone® Gel, 5%, should be applied in a thin layer to acne-affected areas twice daily. The gel should be rubbed in gently and completely, and hands should be washed after application. If no improvement is observed after 12 weeks, the treatment should be reassessed. Common adverse reactions include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, pancreatitis, vertigo, blurred vision, and tinnitus. Serious adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include suicide attempts, tonic-clonic movements, severe abdominal pain, pancreatitis, and severe pharyngitis. Depression and psychosis were also reported in a small number of patients. Local cutaneous events such as oiliness/peeling, dryness, and erythema were the most common side effects observed in clinical studies. Dapsone® Gel, 5%, is contraindicated in patients taking oral dapsone or antimalarial medications due to the potential for hemolytic reactions. It should also not be used in combination with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, as this may increase the likelihood of hemolysis. While no clinically relevant hemolysis or anemia was observed in patients treated with Dapsone® Gel, 5%, some G6PD-deficient individuals showed laboratory changes suggestive of mild hemolysis. If signs or symptoms of hemolytic anemia occur, the gel should be discontinued. Peripheral neuropathy, characterized by motor loss and muscle weakness, has been reported with oral dapsone treatment but was not observed in clinical trials with the topical gel. Similarly, severe skin reactions such as toxic epidermal necrolysis and erythema multiforme, which have been associated with oral dapsone, were not observed with the topical formulation. The mechanism of action of Dapsone® Gel in treating acne vulgaris is not fully understood. No microbiology or immunology studies were conducted during clinical trials, and there is no data on whether dapsone treatment affects the susceptibility of Propionibacterium acnes to other antimicrobials. Therapeutic resistance to dapsone has been reported in Mycobacterium leprae with oral use. Dapsone® Gel, 5%, is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, and animal studies have shown embryocidal effects at high doses, likely secondary to maternal toxicity. The gel should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Dapsone is excreted in human milk, and a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. Safety and efficacy were evaluated in pediatric patients aged 12-17 years, with adverse event rates similar to the vehicle control group. However, the gel is not recommended for use in children under 12 years of age due to a lack of data. Clinical studies did not include sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. Dapsone® Gel, 5%, should be stored at controlled room temperature (20°-25°C or 68°-77°F) and protected from freezing. It is supplied in various tube sizes and should be kept out of reach of children under 12 years old. Patients should use Dapsone® Gel, 5%, as directed by their physician and report any adverse reactions. The gel is for external use only and should not be used for any condition other than that for which it was prescribed. Alcohol interaction with topical dapsone has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while on this medication.
